analysis.one_liner: Requires billionaires and households with over $100 million in income to pay tax on their gains every year.
analysis.headline: Introduced September 17, 2025 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote despite 23 cosponsors — every one a Democrat or independent.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill closes a set of tax rules that let the ultra-wealthy avoid income tax for decades, sometimes forever. Households with more than $100 million in income or $1 billion in assets would pay tax each year on gains in stocks and other tradable assets, even if they never sell — the same way a worker pays tax on each paycheck. Gains in private, hard-to-price assets would be taxed when sold or transferred, plus an interest charge for the years the tax was put off. It would also tax billion-dollar fortunes as if sold when given away or left at death, ending the 'buy, borrow, die' strategy, and close more than 30 other tax breaks used by the ultra-wealthy. Retirement accounts like 401(k)s, IRAs, HSAs, and 529 college plans are excluded.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly and broadly. The bill does not cut anyone's taxes, but it narrows the gap between how wages and billion-dollar investment gains are taxed, reduces the deficit pressure created by untaxed wealth, and preserves the preferential treatment of ordinary retirement savings by explicitly excluding 401(k)s, IRAs, HSAs, 529 plans, and pensions from its scope.

how_it_helps.text: Taxpayers who exceed $100 million in annual income (or hold $1 billion in assets) for three straight years must recognize gains and losses on tradable assets each year as if they had sold them at fair market value, ending indefinite deferral of tax on unrealized gains.

The bill's stated purpose is to shut down 'buy, borrow, die' — the practice of holding appreciating assets, borrowing against them tax-free for living expenses, and passing them on so heirs inherit them free of income tax. It does this by treating covered assets given away, left at death, or placed in trust as sold at fair market value, with exceptions for transfers to spouses and charities.

It closes more than 30 other provisions used by high-net-worth taxpayers, including like-kind real estate exchanges, tax-free exchanges of assets for stock, deferral on certain compensation, private placement life insurance, small business stock exclusions, and qualified opportunity fund loopholes.

Ordinary savings vehicles are excluded from 'covered assets' entirely — 401(k)s, defined benefit pensions, IRAs, HSAs, 529 college plans, ABLE accounts, and Coverdell accounts — so the bill does not touch how working families save.

The bill softens the first year: newly covered taxpayers can pay the first year's extra tax in five annual installments, and startup founders may elect to treat up to $1 billion of stock in a single company as a private asset taxed on transfer rather than marked to market annually.

analysis.who_pays: Households with more than $100 million in yearly income or $1 billion in assets would pay substantially more tax each year, and the advisors who sell them deferral and estate-planning strategies would lose business. There is no provision in the bill that raises anyone else's taxes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Billion-dollar households and their tax advisors

drawbacks.text: Annual tax on assets that were never sold creates liquidity problems: an owner of a rising private company or illiquid asset could owe tax on paper gains without cash on hand to pay it, potentially forcing sales.

Private, hard-to-value assets are not marked to market at all; instead the tax is deferred until the asset is sold or transferred, with an interest charge capped at 49% of the gain — so wealthy holders of private companies can still put off paying tax for years, paying only an interest premium on top.

Valuation of nontradable assets relies on multiple competing methods — original cost, adjusted basis, financial statements, loan collateral values — which invites disputes and litigation over what a private asset is worth.

Taxing the mere holding of an asset as a taxable event raises constitutional challenges under the Sixteenth Amendment that courts have not yet settled for mark-to-market schemes, and critics argue the tax could push ultra-wealthy taxpayers to move assets or expatriate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a narrow slice of the population (the thresholds reach only households above $100 million in income or $1 billion in assets, tested over three years) while addressing a real inequity: gains on wealth are taxed only when sold, or never, while wages are taxed every year. The design shows real effort to avoid the obvious pitfalls — retirement accounts are carved out, the first-year hit can be spread over five years, founders get a limited election, and private-asset gains get a deferred-with-interest regime instead of annual marking. The main honest criticisms are the valuation burden for private assets, the liquidity squeeze an annual unrealized-gains tax can create, and the fact that nontradable assets still escape annual taxation altogether. It is a substantial but carefully hedged bill, not a blanket wealth tax.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2025 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the two-year Congress still has time left.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the Billionaires Income Tax Act on September 17, 2025; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The complete action history shows no activity after the referral — no hearing, no committee report, no floor action through the remainder of the record.
The bill has 23 cosponsors, all of them Senate Democrats or independents; 22 of the Senate's 45 Democrats and 1 of its 2 independents signed on. No Republican is listed.
Republicans hold 55 of the 100 Senate seats and control the Finance Committee's agenda, and the bill's provisions would apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with billion-dollar fortunes keep paying little or no annual income tax on their unrealized gains, and the tax-planning, estate-planning, and wealth management industries keep selling them deferral strategies. Ordinary taxpayers are neither better nor worse off yet, because the bill has not become law.

industries.note: These households would owe tax annually on tradable gains, an interest charge on deferred private-asset gains, and tax on assets given away or inherited — ending 'buy, borrow, die'. Their gain in the status quo is unpaid tax that ordinary wage earners make up through the deficit.

industries.industry: Estate planning and tax advisory services
industries.note: The bill explicitly targets the deferral and estate-planning strategies these firms sell — buy-borrow-die, grantor trusts, stock swaps, and life insurance wrappers — threatening a core line of business serving the ultra-wealthy.

industries.industry: Private company owners and private equity investors
industries.note: Private, nontradable holdings escape annual mark-to-market and face tax only on sale or transfer, plus a capped interest charge — a softer regime than public-stock holders get. Billion-dollar founders also get a one-time election to defer treatment on up to $1 billion of stock in one company.

industries.industry: Private placement life insurance and annuity providers
industries.note: The bill strips the special tax treatment of these contracts for applicable taxpayers and requires the cash surrender value to reflect underlying investments, closing a favored vehicle for sheltering investment gains.
QOF holdings held by applicable taxpayers are reclassified as nontradable assets with modified breaks, limiting a vehicle used to defer and reduce capital gains.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in a Finance Committee chaired by a Republican whose caucus holds 55 Senate seats, and no Republican has cosponsored. Billionaire tax proposals from Democratic sponsors have historically not received markups in divided Senates. Absent an unexpected Democratic capture of the chamber or a decision to attach the bill to a broader tax package, it is likely to remain in committee without a vote for the rest of this Congress.
